statements.quote: The other chapters of this course trace two of the three legs that hold up a large language model: the **ideas** (the syllogism, the number, the proof, the token) and the **matter** (the sand, the wire, the transistor, the cooling fluid, the grid of power).
statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: But a model is not a thing that thinks; it is a thing that a mind *built*.
statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: And the mind that built it is the deepest, least visible, and most "displaced" of all the prerequisites on this site.
statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: Every technique that looks, from the outside, like a modern invention of AI turns out to be an **externalization** or an **emulation** of a capacity that evolved long before the first silicon die, for foraging, for social life, and for staying alive.
statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: The brain is, in effect, the **first large language model**: a predictive, generative, loss-minimizing, embodied, social, world-modeling engine that runs on a few tens of watts of wet tissue.
statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: What we have done, in building LLMs, is not to invent a new kind of mind.
statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: We have taken a few of the oldest tricks in the animal book and re-implemented them in silicon, then scaled them past anything biology could afford.
statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: This chapter follows that thread as far down as the evidence allows.
statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: It is, like the material history that precedes it, a history of **exaptation**: the taking-over of a structure for a purpose it was never designed for.
statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: The jaws that became the ear bones, the social mind-reading that learned to model electrons, the forager's appetite that became the scientist's curiosity.

statements.section: The Displaced Prerequisite of All Displaced Prerequisites

statements.quote: A human brain is roughly two per cent of body mass yet consumes close to a quarter of the body's resting energy.

statements.quote: For millions of years our ancestors had a brain of roughly ape-size, and the central puzzle of human evolution is how the species could *afford* to triple it.
statements.section: The Expensive Brain

statements.quote: The **expensive-tissue hypothesis** of \citeauthorlastnameand{aiellowheeler1995expensivetissue} offers the most economical accounting: the brain could only be paid for by *spending less* elsewhere, and the organ that gave up the most was the gut.
statements.section: The Expensive Brain

statements.quote: A larger, more expensive brain and a smaller, cheaper digestive tract are, on this account, two sides of the same metabolic coin, and the shift that made both possible was the move to **cooking**.
statements.section: The Expensive Brain

statements.quote: \citeauthor{wrangham2009catching} argues in \citetitle{wrangham2009catching} that the controlled use of fire — a turning point already discussed in the material history — did more than protect and gather.
statements.section: The Expensive Brain

statements.quote: By pre-digesting food, cooking made a far greater share of calories available per mouthful, which let the gut shrink and the brain expand.
statements.section: The Expensive Brain

statements.quote: This is where the history of **energy** and the history of **cognition** quietly meet: the caloric surplus of the hearth is what bought the first cognitive surplus.
statements.section: The Expensive Brain

statements.quote: There is no abstract thought in a body that must spend all its fuel on digesting raw tubers.
statements.section: The Expensive Brain

statements.quote: The "need" that made AI possible was, at the deepest level, a **budget line item in an ancient metabolizing animal**.

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{dunbar2012socialbrain} and others have long noted that across primates the size of the neocortex scales with the **size of the social group** an individual must track: who is allied with whom, who owes what to whom, who is a threat, who is a mate.

statements.quote: Managing a society of hundreds is a combinatorial problem of staggering difficulty, and the "currency" in which it is managed is **information about other minds**.
statements.section: The Social Brain

statements.quote: \citeauthor{dunbar2012socialbrain} proposed that **language** itself evolved, at least in part, as a "vocal grooming" technology, a way to maintain and manipulate those social bonds at a distance and in parallel, the way a chimp can groom only one individual at a time.
statements.section: The Social Brain

statements.quote: The brain that made AI possible was, first and foremost, a **social** brain, and the "theory of mind" — the capacity to model what others know, want, and believe — is its signature achievement.

statements.quote: In the "free-energy" and "predictive-processing" programs associated with \citeauthor{friston2010freeenergy}, the brain maintains an internal generative model of the world and is driven, at every moment, to **minimize the surprise** — the prediction error — between its model and its sensory input.
statements.section: The Predictive Brain

statements.quote: Perception, on this view, is a top-down hypothesis test: the cortex sends down a prediction, the eyes send back the mismatch, and the weights are nudged to reduce the mismatch.
statements.section: The Predictive Brain

statements.quote: This is not a metaphor that merely *rhymes* with machine learning.
statements.section: The Predictive Brain

statements.quote: A neural network in training is a generative model whose parameters are updated to **minimize a loss function**, and the brain is a generative model whose synapses are updated to minimize a **prediction error**.
statements.section: The Predictive Brain

statements.quote: The "loss" that gradient descent descends is, in the nervous system, the "surprise" that the nervous system is wired to drive toward zero.
statements.section: The Predictive Brain

statements.quote: When you watch a Transformer's training curve fall, you are watching, in slow motion and on a different substrate, exactly the process a forager's brain runs to survive the next hour.
statements.section: The Predictive Brain

statements.quote: The entire edifice of "learning from data" was invented by evolution before the word *data* existed.
statements.section: The Predictive Brain

statements.quote: There is, however, a cruel constraint on all of this: the mind has almost no **scratch space**.
statements.section: The Working-Memory Bottleneck

statements.quote: \citeauthor{miller1956magicalnumber} famously found that the number of discrete items a person can hold "in mind" at once is small and stubborn, around **seven plus or minus two** chunks, and that this limit is remarkably stable across tasks — though later work puts the raw-item limit nearer four (\cite[Cowan, 2001]{cowan2001magical4}).
statements.section: The Working-Memory Bottleneck

statements.quote: This is one of the most load-bearing facts in the whole history of the mind, because a tiny working buffer is precisely the condition that *forces* a mind to **compress**.
statements.section: The Working-Memory Bottleneck

statements.quote: You cannot hold everything, so you must group, summarize, and abstract, and the groups you form become the units you think with.
statements.section: The Working-Memory Bottleneck

statements.quote: The bottleneck is not a bug of the human mind; it is the very pressure that pushed it to build the "extra level of indirection" this whole course is about.
statements.section: The Working-Memory Bottleneck

statements.quote: Without the cramped working memory, there would be no need for the chunk, the category, the symbol — and no need, in the end, for the token.
statements.section: The Working-Memory Bottleneck

statements.quote: The mechanism by which the mind escapes its working-memory bottleneck is **chunking**.
statements.section: Chunking: Compressing the World into Usable Units

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{chasesimon1973chess} showed, in a now-classic study of chess perception, that a chess master looks at a board and does not see thirty-two separate pieces but a small number of **familiar configurations**, and that this chunking, not raw visual acuity, is what makes the master "see" a position in an instant.
statements.section: Chunking: Compressing the World into Usable Units

statements.quote: Experts in any domain are experts because they have **compressed** their field into a library of reusable units.
statements.section: Chunking: Compressing the World into Usable Units

statements.quote: This is the cognitive origin of the token.
statements.section: Chunking: Compressing the World into Usable Units

statements.quote: A tokenizer does not understand language; it does what a chess master's eye does, it **chunks** a stream of symbols into a manageable number of meaningful pieces, and a pre-trained model does what the master's memory does, it **retrieves** the configurations that matter.
statements.section: Chunking: Compressing the World into Usable Units

statements.quote: The "vocabulary" of a transformer is a chunking scheme, and the "context window" is a working-memory limit.
statements.section: Chunking: Compressing the World into Usable Units

statements.quote: The whole architecture is a confession that the mind cannot hold it all, so it must reduce the world to a few hundred reusable symbols and reason over those.
statements.section: Chunking: Compressing the World into Usable Units

statements.quote: To chunk, a mind must **categorize**, and human categorization turned out to be far less crisp than logic textbooks assumed.
statements.section: Categories, Prototypes, and Fuzzy Boundaries

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{rosch1975familyresemblance} showed that the members of a natural category are not separated from non-members by a clean boundary but graded around a **prototype**: some chairs are "more chair" than others, some birds are "more bird", and a category is a **cloud** in a space of similarity rather than a region fenced off by a definition.
statements.section: Categories, Prototypes, and Fuzzy Boundaries

statements.quote: A category is best understood as a region of a **geometry**, with a center, a spread, and fuzzy, gradient edges.
statements.section: Categories, Prototypes, and Fuzzy Boundaries

statements.quote: That geometry is not a loose analogy; it is the ancestor of the **embedding space** in which a modern model lives.
statements.section: Categories, Prototypes, and Fuzzy Boundaries

statements.quote: When a language model places "king" near "queen" and "man" near "woman", it is doing, in a high-dimensional vector space, exactly what a human categorizer does around a prototype: it is learning that the world is organized into **clouds of related things**, and that the distance between two points in the cloud carries meaning.
statements.section: Categories, Prototypes, and Fuzzy Boundaries

statements.quote: The "fuzzy boundary" that Rosch found in a child's idea of a "chair" is the same fuzzy boundary that makes a soft nearest-neighbor in an embedding space more useful than a hard one.
statements.section: Categories, Prototypes, and Fuzzy Boundaries

statements.quote: Semantic space is the geometry of human categories, made explicit.
statements.section: Categories, Prototypes, and Fuzzy Boundaries

statements.quote: If chunking is compression, then **analogy** is the mind's engine of *invention*.
statements.section: Analogy: The Engine of Discovery

statements.quote: The philosopher and AI researcher \citeauthor{gentner1983structuremapping} proposed that we understand a new thing by **mapping the relational structure** of a thing we already know onto it: we do not copy surface features, we copy *relationships*.
statements.section: Analogy: The Engine of Discovery

statements.quote: A heart is "like a pump" not because it is red and wet, but because it takes an input, moves a fluid, and resists back-pressure.
statements.section: Analogy: The Engine of Discovery

statements.quote: Analogy is structure-mapping, and it is, arguably, the single most important cognitive tool the mind owns.
statements.section: Analogy: The Engine of Discovery

statements.quote: Every great scientific advance in this course's history is an analogy that someone dared to make explicit: the atom as a tiny solar system, the electric current as a flow of water, the nervous system as a telegraph, the universe as a clockwork, the cell as a factory.
statements.section: Analogy: The Engine of Discovery

statements.quote: The "mathematical" and the "physical" parts of AI are both built from analogies: a differential equation that "behave like" a physical system, a probability that "acts like" a frequency, a gradient that "rolls downhill" through a landscape.

statements.quote: To build an LLM is to chain together a few very powerful analogies — that *language is a sequence*, that *a sequence is a probability*, that *a probability can be optimized* — and the human mind's native fluency in analogical structure is what let anyone see that the chain could be closed.
statements.section: Analogy: The Engine of Discovery

statements.quote: Even the most abstract of our ideas, it turns out, are **down in the body**.

statements.quote: The "up and down" of a number line is in the motor and spatial cortex before it is in the algebra.
statements.section: Metaphor and the Embodied Mind

statements.quote: The mind built the body's metaphors first and the mathematics second, and the mathematics is, at bottom, the metaphor made rigorous.
statements.section: Metaphor and the Embodied Mind

statements.quote: A mind that can only *look at* a representation is limited to the views it has already been given.

statements.quote: The human mind can **manipulate** a representation — and the cleanest proof came in 1971, when \citeauthorlastnameand{shepardmetzler1971} showed that people can *rotate* a three-dimensional object in their heads.

statements.quote: The experiment: subjects were shown two 3-D assemblies of cubes, drawn in different orientations, and asked only "same or different?" statements.quote: One step stands above all the others, and it is the step that makes **formal systems** possible at all: the ability to **think about one's own thinking**.

statements.quote: \citeauthor{flavell1979metacognition} named this capacity **metacognition**, the "cognitive monitoring" by which a mind holds a representation of its own representations and can inspect, correct, and report on them.

statements.quote: It is the "stepping outside" that the introduction's "ladder of abstraction" gestures toward, and it is what separates a reflex from a *deliberation*.

statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: The `int` in your code is the descendant of a primate's "a lot" and "a few", made exact.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: Every number a machine manipulates is, in its origin, a body's fuzzy sense of quantity, refined across millennia until it could be trusted with a nuclear calculation.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: The approximate number sense has a sharp **ceiling**, and knowing where it is reveals what counting actually *adds*.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: For a small set of objects — up to about **four** — you do not count at all; you **subitize**: you *see* the number, instantly, in a single glance, the way you see a single object \cite[subitizing]{subitizing}.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: Show a child three dots or five dots and the judgment "more" is immediate for three but not for five; three and five straddle a wall.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: Beyond the subitizing limit, the mind switches to a **serial process** — counting one, two, three, four, five — which is slower and can be interrupted or lost.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: So "counting" is not the same thing as "knowing how many"; it is the *procedure* you reach for once the fast, parallel intuition runs out.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: The boundary is not just a lab curiosity; it is a window into **whether exact number ever needs language at all**.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: In two of the few studied communities without exact number words — the Pirahã of the Amazon, whose lexicon has no words for specific quantities, and the Mundurucú, who have number words only up to a small value before a word like "many" \cite[Pirahã (Gordon, 2004); Pica et al., Mundurucú (2004)]{piraha2004, picamundurucu2004} — the tests reveal the same architecture: an approximate, ratio-sensitive sense that *works* up to a small magnitude and then **breaks**.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: The Mundurucú can compare and even add large numbers *approximately* — is this group of 50 bigger than that group of 40?
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: — but ask them for the *exact* sum once their number words run out, and accuracy collapses.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: Exact arithmetic, it turns out, is not an innate sense waiting to be switched on; it is a **construction** — the approximate intuition, sharpened by the scaffolding of exact number words and counting.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: That is the bridge from the forager's "a lot" to the `int` in your code: not a jump, but a tool that makes an intuition exact.
statements.section: The Number Sense

statements.quote: Among the strangest capacities of a young mind is its insistence on **play** — activity with no immediate payoff, repeated for its own sake.
statements.section: Play: Rehearsal for the Novel

statements.quote: Research connecting evolutionary psychology, child development, and creativity has argued that play is not a frivolous by-product but a **practice environment**: a low-stakes arena in which a young animal or child can try combinations, test cause and effect, and role-play situations it will meet only later and more dangerously.
statements.section: Play: Rehearsal for the Novel

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{mehta2020play} review this "play deficit" line of work and its link to creativity, the idea that the ability to *play with ideas* is a core ingredient of the flexible, novel thinking that culture rewards.
statements.section: Play: Rehearsal for the Novel

statements.quote: For a history of AI, play is load-bearing in a way that is easy to miss.
statements.section: Play: Rehearsal for the Novel

statements.quote: The "useful" part of any breakthrough — the theorem, the algorithm, the architecture — is almost always *found* during the "useless" part: the idle fiddling, the toy example, the puzzle solved for the sheer pleasure of solving it.
statements.section: Play: Rehearsal for the Novel

statements.quote: The reason a culture of "researchers" can exist at all is that humans, unlike most animals, will pursue a problem **for the fun of it**, long before its value is clear.
statements.section: Play: Rehearsal for the Novel

statements.quote: Basic science, the "curiosity-driven" work that produced logic, number theory, and probability, is institutionalized play.
statements.section: Play: Rehearsal for the Novel

statements.quote: A society that funds only what is immediately practical does not, by definition, discover the next thing.
statements.section: Play: Rehearsal for the Novel

statements.quote: The engine of the "useless" mind is one of the great, invisible, cultural prerequisites of AI.
statements.section: Play: Rehearsal for the Novel

statements.quote: Play is powered by a specific and well-studied appetite: **curiosity**.
statements.section: Curiosity and the Intrinsic Drive

statements.quote: \citeauthor{loewenstein1994curiosity} reframed curiosity as a drive to close a gap between what one knows and what one *wants* to know, an "information gap" that is aversive to leave open and rewarding to close.
statements.section: Curiosity and the Intrinsic Drive

statements.quote: Crucially, this drive can run **independently of any external reward**: a mind will chase an answer it has no use for.
statements.section: Curiosity and the Intrinsic Drive

statements.quote: This "intrinsic motivation" is the fuel of science, and it is a genuinely strange evolutionary product, a mechanism that spends energy on questions whose survival value is not obvious.
statements.section: Curiosity and the Intrinsic Drive

statements.quote: An LLM does not get curious.
statements.section: Curiosity and the Intrinsic Drive

statements.quote: It is given a task and optimized toward a reward, which is precisely why "intrinsic motivation" is one of the most discussed open problems in modern AI, and why the "self-improving" agents on the frontier are, in effect, attempts to *build* into a system the one drive the human brain got for free.
statements.section: Curiosity and the Intrinsic Drive

statements.quote: The gap between the two — the model that wants to be told what to do, and the scientist who wants to be left alone to wonder — is a gap between a **reinforcement** system and a **curiosity** system, and closing it is a matter of importing, into silicon, the oldest appetite in the social brain.
statements.section: Curiosity and the Intrinsic Drive

statements.quote: Some of the most important thinking does not happen when a mind is *focused* on a problem, but when it has set the problem **aside**.
statements.section: Incubation, Daydreaming, and the "Aha"

statements.quote: The classic "stages of creative insight" — preparation, **incubation**, illumination, and verification — were laid out a century ago and remain the standard description.
statements.section: Incubation, Daydreaming, and the "Aha"

statements.quote: The psychologist \citeauthor{mednick1962creative} modeled the "aha" as a process of **associative combination**: the mind, during the unfocused incubation phase, keeps loosely and randomly recombining the pieces of the problem, until a new, useful connection happens to fire.
statements.section: Incubation, Daydreaming, and the "Aha"

statements.quote: The insight, when it strikes, is usually a **recombination** the focused mind could never have found, because the focused mind is too locked onto the obvious path.
statements.section: Incubation, Daydreaming, and the "Aha"

statements.quote: There is now strong evidence for where this happens in the brain.
statements.section: Incubation, Daydreaming, and the "Aha"

statements.quote: The **default-mode network**, identified by \citeauthorlastnameand{raichle2007defaultmode} as the set of regions that are *active* when the mind is not doing an external task — the "daydreaming" circuit — is precisely the circuit that lights up during recall, imagination, and self-referential thought.
statements.section: Incubation, Daydreaming, and the "Aha"

statements.quote: The shower-thought, the insight on the walk, the answer that arrives in the night, are the default mode doing its slow, loose, low-cost search over the space of possibilities.
statements.section: Incubation, Daydreaming, and the "Aha"

statements.quote: The "unconscious" is not a place where thought goes to die; it is a **background process**, and it is, in a sense, the first form of **asynchronous computation**, a computation that runs while the "foreground" is doing something else.

statements.quote: The mathematician's famous "let me sleep on it" is a scheduling decision.
statements.section: Incubation, Daydreaming, and the "Aha"

statements.quote: A mind that can only model the world *as it is* is a mind that cannot plan.
statements.section: Imagination, Counterfactuals, and Fiction

statements.quote: The human mind's signature extra is the ability to model the world **as it might be**: to run **counterfactuals**, to simulate "what if".
statements.section: Imagination, Counterfactuals, and Fiction

statements.quote: This is the same machinery as imagination, and it is the machinery that makes planning, design, and **fiction** possible.
statements.section: Imagination, Counterfactuals, and Fiction

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{tomasello2014thinking} argues that the distinctive human move is not just to model the world, but to model it **together**, in a shared, "we" mode, and that the shared fictional world — the story, the myth, the scenario everyone agrees to treat as "real for the moment" — is a technology of coordination as powerful as any tool.
statements.section: Imagination, Counterfactuals, and Fiction

statements.quote: Fiction is, in this light, a form of **counterfactual training data**.
statements.section: Imagination, Counterfactuals, and Fiction

statements.quote: Before a society could build a ship, it could *imagine* the ship, rehearse its operation in story, and agree on the roles.
statements.section: Imagination, Counterfactuals, and Fiction

statements.quote: Before a civilization could run a large-scale project, it had to be able to hold a **shared hypothetical** in common.
statements.section: Imagination, Counterfactuals, and Fiction

statements.quote: The "imagination" that makes AI possible, the ability to model a state of the world that does not yet exist and to act on that model, is the same imagination that made the first story, the first plan, and the first "what if we tried it this way?" possible.
statements.section: Imagination, Counterfactuals, and Fiction

statements.quote: A language model is, at bottom, a machine for generating counterfactuals of text, and it inherited the capacity from the mind that first dared to imagine a sentence that had never been said.
statements.section: Imagination, Counterfactuals, and Fiction

statements.section: Art and the Symbolic Revolution

statements.quote: The decorated ochre and complex tools documented from sites such as Blombos Cave, and the painted walls of caves in Europe, are the earliest surviving artifacts of a mind that can represent **something that is not present**, a mind that can make a mark *stand for* a thing.

statements.quote: (\cite[Henshilwood et al., 2002]{emergenceofmodernhumanbehaviour}) This is the first **generative model** we have direct evidence for: a system for producing and sharing representations of a world beyond the immediate.

statements.section: Art and the Symbolic Revolution

statements.quote: The oldest surviving "document" is, in this sense, an externalized memory of an absent mind.
statements.section: Art and the Symbolic Revolution

statements.quote: The connection to AI is not that a cave painting "was" a neural network.
statements.section: Art and the Symbolic Revolution

statements.quote: It is that the *capacity* demonstrated in the painting — to build an internal model of the world, to render parts of it in a durable medium, and to share the rendering with others — is the same capacity, pushed to an extreme, that a language model now performs over text.
statements.section: Art and the Symbolic Revolution

statements.quote: The forager who painted a horse had, in miniature, built a world model and externalized a piece of it.
statements.section: Art and the Symbolic Revolution

statements.quote: The model that now generates a thousand horses at a time has scaled that same move until the "cave wall" is a vector space and the "pigment" is a probability distribution.

statements.quote: The Greeks did not begin their science with a hypothesis; they began with a feeling.
statements.section: From Wonder to Philosophy

statements.quote: In the opening of the *Metaphysics*, \citeauthor{aristotlemetaphysics} writes that the pursuit of understanding begins in **wonder** (Greek: *thaumazein*), the felt strangeness of the fact that things are the way they are.
statements.section: From Wonder to Philosophy

statements.quote: "It is through wonder that men now begin and once began to philosophize," he says, and from the wonder at particular things the mind is drawn, step by step, to the question of the whole.
statements.section: From Wonder to Philosophy

statements.quote: This single sentence is the oldest statement in the history of science, and it locates the origin of the scientific mind not in a method but in an **emotion**: the discomfort of not-understanding, and the pleasure of resolving it.
statements.section: From Wonder to Philosophy

statements.quote: \citealternativetitle{aristotleandplato} (detail) — Aristotle, at right, in Raphael's *Scuola di Atene*: the philosopher who located the origin of science in the felt discomfort of not-understanding.
statements.section: From Wonder to Philosophy

statements.quote: That emotion is the same one as curiosity, and the same one as the "information gap".
statements.section: From Wonder to Philosophy

statements.quote: The "ideengeschichte" of science, the history of the *idea* of science, begins with the decision to take the feeling of wonder **seriously**, to treat a puzzled mind as a mind that *ought* to be unpuzzled, and to treat the resolution of that puzzle as worth doing for its own sake.
statements.section: From Wonder to Philosophy

statements.quote: Every later "scientific method" is a technology for managing that original discomfort: a way to make wonder productive, to aim it, to check it, and to make the un-puzzled mind reliable enough to build on.
statements.section: From Wonder to Philosophy

statements.quote: Wonder is qualitative; **mathematics** is what made it quantitative, and that was a cultural invention of enormous and easily-overlooked consequence.
statements.section: The Quantitative Turn

statements.quote: \citeauthor{daston1988probability} has traced how, in the Enlightenment, the very idea of what counts as *knowledge* changed: from a kind of qualitative, rhetorical certainty to a **quantified, probabilistic** certainty in which statements are graded by likelihood and uncertainty is a number one can manipulate.
statements.section: The Quantitative Turn

statements.quote: The "scientific" attitude, on this account, is not just "looking carefully" but **looking numerically**, a shift in the *epistemic* — in what a mind is allowed to count as a good reason.
statements.section: The Quantitative Turn

statements.quote: The reason this is a prerequisite of AI is that modern machine learning is, at its core, a **quantified** practice.
statements.section: The Quantitative Turn

statements.quote: A model does not "believe" a statement; it assigns it a **probability**.
statements.section: The Quantitative Turn

statements.quote: It does not "know" the answer; it computes a **distribution**.
statements.section: The Quantitative Turn

statements.quote: The entire machinery of the cross-entropy loss, the softmax, the "confidence" of a prediction, is the Enlightenment's quantification of uncertainty pushed to its limit.
statements.section: The Quantitative Turn

statements.quote: Before a machine could be *trained*, a culture had to decide that the world was the kind of place where things could be **counted, measured, and predicted**, and that doing so was a legitimate and even superior way of knowing.
statements.section: The Quantitative Turn

statements.quote: That decision is a historical and psychological one, not a logical one.
statements.section: The Quantitative Turn

statements.quote: The turning point of that quantification is often placed with \citeauthor{galileoassayer1623}, who wrote, in *The Assayer* (*Il Saggiatore*, 1623), that the "book of nature" is "written in the language of mathematics" and that its characters are "triangles, circles, and other geometric figures, without which it is humanly impossible to understand a single word of it." Here is the deepest single "idea" in the entire history of science, and it is not a discovery of a *fact* about the world but a **commitment about how to read** the world: the claim that the structure of reality is, at bottom, **geometric and quantitative**, and that to understand a thing is to find its shape.
statements.section: "The Book of Nature Is Written in the Language of Mathematics"

statements.quote: \citealternativetitle{galilei_image} — Galileo, from Justus Sustermans's 1636 portrait (Uffizi), who bet that the "book of nature" was written in the language of mathematics.
statements.section: "The Book of Nature Is Written in the Language of Mathematics"

statements.quote: It is worth dwelling on this, because it is the idea that made AI *thinkable*.
statements.section: "The Book of Nature Is Written in the Language of Mathematics"

statements.quote: The assumption that the world has a **formal structure** that can be *discovered* and *manipulated symbolically* is the assumption that a machine can one day be made to do the discovering.
statements.section: "The Book of Nature Is Written in the Language of Mathematics"

statements.quote: If nature is a text written in mathematics, then a machine that manipulates mathematics is, in principle, a machine that can *read nature*.
statements.section: "The Book of Nature Is Written in the Language of Mathematics"

statements.quote: Every theorem prover, every symbolic system, every "the world as a model" is a downstream consequence of Galileo's commitment.
statements.section: "The Book of Nature Is Written in the Language of Mathematics"

statements.quote: The history of AI is, at this level, the history of a single wager, made in the seventeenth century, that the world is legible by a formal language, and that a sufficiently clever reader could be built out of the same symbols.
statements.section: "The Book of Nature Is Written in the Language of Mathematics"

statements.quote: How, then, does a human *find* a new piece of that formal structure?
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: The most important first-person account in the history of the subject is \citeauthor{poincare1910creation}'s *Mathematical Creation*, in which he describes, with unusual honesty, how his own breakthroughs actually happened.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: Not by grinding, but by a **preparation** of intense effort, followed by a period when he deliberately *stopped* working on the problem and let his mind wander, followed by a sudden **illumination** — a combination that appeared "out of nowhere", in an instant, and was then checked by conscious work.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: Poincaré reported that the **unconscious** mind was doing the combinatorial search: it tried countless combinations of ideas while he slept or walked, and delivered only the ones that fit, for him to verify.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: \citealternativetitle{poincare_image} — Henri Poincaré, who in *Mathematical Creation* described how his breakthroughs arrived by unconscious recombination, not grinding.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: This is the "aha" of the earlier section, now applied to the highest form of abstract thought.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: And it carries a second, subtler insight: Poincaré emphasized that the unconscious search is **guided by an aesthetic**.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: The mind does not accept every combination that fits; it is drawn to the ones that are **simple, symmetric, and "beautiful"**, and that aesthetic is, in effect, a heuristic for **compression** — the elegant proof is the *short* proof, the one with the least redundant description.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: There is a deep reason mathematicians chase beauty: beauty is a shadow of **low complexity**, of the short program that generates the pattern, and chasing the short description is a reliable (if never guaranteed) way to find the *right* abstraction.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: The "taste" of the mathematician is an intuition for Kolmogorov complexity, for the ratio of a pattern's information to the length of the rule that makes it.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: \citeauthor{polya1945solve} later systematized the *conscious* side of this — the heuristics, the "how to attack a problem" — but the engine, Poincaré showed, was the loose, aesthetic, **offline** search that the focused mind cannot perform.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: \citeauthor{penrose1989emperor} took this first-person picture seriously and drew a much stronger conclusion from it.

statements.quote: In \citetitle{penrose1989emperor} (\citeyear{penrose1989emperor}) he argues that mathematical *understanding* is not algorithmic.
statements.section: The Psychology of Mathematical Discovery

statements.quote: A human mathematician can, he claims, recognize the truth of a Gödel sentence—a true arithmetic statement that a given formal system can neither prove nor refute—so no formal system can capture what the mathematician does.

statements.quote: He also speculated that the missing ingredient might lie in a future, non-computable theory of quantum gravity, a proposal that remains speculative.

statements.quote: Either way, the “compression” story of mathematical beauty is incomplete as a theory of mathematical *insight*: it describes the shape of the short proof, not the act of seeing that it must be true.

statements.quote: One of the most important ideas in the psychology of decision-making, and one of the most under-appreciated prerequisites of *engineering*, comes from \citeauthor{simon1955bounded}.
statements.section: Satisficing: The Practical, "Good Enough" Mind

statements.quote: Simon argued that real minds do not **optimize** — they cannot, because the problem is too large and the information too incomplete — and that instead they **satisfice**: they search until they find a solution that is *good enough*, and then they stop.
statements.section: Satisficing: The Practical, "Good Enough" Mind

statements.quote: The "rational" agent of the textbooks is a fiction; the real agent is a **bounded** one, working with limited memory and time, and choosing the first acceptable option.
statements.section: Satisficing: The Practical, "Good Enough" Mind

statements.quote: This is the psychological root of the **practicality** that the whole course keeps returning to.
statements.section: Satisficing: The Practical, "Good Enough" Mind

statements.quote: Engineering is the art of satisficing: not the optimal design, but the *good-enough* design that can actually be built, by real people, with real materials, on real deadlines.
statements.section: Satisficing: The Practical, "Good Enough" Mind

statements.quote: The "bitter lesson" of AI, that brute scaling beats hand-crafted cleverness, is a satisficing story at the level of the whole field: the field kept choosing the *good enough* brute method over the *elegant* hand-tuned one, because the brute method was the one that could be *built*.

statements.quote: The practical, "stop when it's good enough" mindset is not a failure of rigor; it is a description of how minds — and civilizations — actually make decisions, and it is why AI is full of "good enough" choices (a good-enough tokenizer, a good-enough approximation, a good-enough heuristic) stacked into something that works.
statements.section: Satisficing: The Practical, "Good Enough" Mind

statements.quote: The mind that built AI is not one brain; it is a **culture**, and the distinctive human trait is not that our brains are large but that our cultures **accumulate**.

statements.quote: \citeauthor{henrich2016secret} argues in \citetitle{henrich2016secret} that human "smarts" are mostly **cultural**, that we are, in his phrase, "cognitively niche-constructing" animals who build an external world of tools and ideas, and that the individual human brain has *evolved* in part to make use of that accumulated knowledge.
statements.section: Cumulative Cultural Evolution and the Ratchet

statements.quote: The key mechanism is the **ratchet effect**: an innovation, once made, can be kept, copied, improved, and passed on, so that each generation starts from where the last one *ended* rather than from scratch.
statements.section: Cumulative Cultural Evolution and the Ratchet

statements.quote: This is the "iterative innovation" that makes AI possible, and it is a cultural, not a biological, fact.
statements.section: Cumulative Cultural Evolution and the Ratchet

statements.quote: A chimpanzee population does not ratchet: a clever trick dies with the chimp who invented it.
statements.section: Cumulative Cultural Evolution and the Ratchet

statements.quote: The "training data" of a modern model is, in the deepest sense, the **ratcheted output of hundreds of thousands of generations** of human iteration, all of it compressed into a corpus.
statements.section: Cumulative Cultural Evolution and the Ratchet

statements.quote: The model is not learning *from nothing*; it is learning from the accumulated, ratcheted, improved-upon work of the species.
statements.section: Cumulative Cultural Evolution and the Ratchet

statements.quote: The "cultural brain" is the first and most important "data set" in the history of intelligence.
statements.section: Cumulative Cultural Evolution and the Ratchet

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{tomasello2014thinking} argues that the specifically human kind of thinking is not just *individual* cognition but **shared** intentionality: the ability to engage with others in a common goal, a common attention, a "we" project, rather than just a parallel set of "I" projects.
statements.section: Shared Intentionality and "We-Mode" Thinking

statements.quote: A human does not just *see* the same thing as a fellow human; she sees it **with** them, and the act of joint attention creates a common ground from which new, collaborative thought can grow.
statements.section: Shared Intentionality and "We-Mode" Thinking

statements.quote: It is this "we-mode" that makes **teaching, learning from others, and cumulative culture** possible in the first place.
statements.section: Shared Intentionality and "We-Mode" Thinking

statements.quote: For AI, the relevance is the "social" in "social learning" and the "shared" in "shared representations".
statements.section: Shared Intentionality and "We-Mode" Thinking

statements.quote: A model trained on the output of many minds is, in a sense, a **collective mind**: it carries the shared biases, the common ground, the "we" assumptions of the culture that produced its training data.
statements.section: Shared Intentionality and "We-Mode" Thinking

statements.quote: The "alignment" problem, the problem of making a model *share* a community's values and goals, is a direct descendant of the problem of shared intentionality: how do two minds, or a mind and a machine, get to the same "we"?
statements.section: Shared Intentionality and "We-Mode" Thinking

statements.quote: The fact that the human mind was built to *coordinate with other minds* is what makes the "interface" between a model and its users even possible, and it is why a model that "gets" the user is not just pattern-matching but, in a loose and important sense, **reading a mind**.
statements.section: Shared Intentionality and "We-Mode" Thinking

statements.quote: The final, and perhaps deepest, move is the **externalization** of the mind.
statements.section: Externalized Memory and the Extended Mind

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{clarkchalmers1998extended} proposed the "extended mind" thesis: that the boundary of a mind does not have to be the skull, that a notebook, a set of notes, a physical artifact that a person *reliably* uses as a part of her thinking, can count as a genuine part of her cognition, on a par with a memory in the head.
statements.section: Externalized Memory and the Extended Mind

statements.quote: The **abacus** in [the untold history](untold_history_ii), the **writing system**, the **book**, the **map** and the **ledger** are all, on this account, parts of the mind that have been placed outside the body.
statements.section: Externalized Memory and the Extended Mind

statements.quote: This is the direct intellectual ancestor of the **vector database** and the **retrieval** system.
statements.section: Externalized Memory and the Extended Mind

statements.quote: A large language model with a memory, an RAG setup, a "context" that reaches outside the model into a corpus, is a **Clark-and-Chalmers extended mind** made literal: a mind whose scratch space is not just a few tokens but a searchable archive of the species' accumulated ratcheted work.
statements.section: Externalized Memory and the Extended Mind

statements.quote: The trajectory is continuous: from the ochre mark on the cave wall (externalized memory of a single image), to the clay tablet (externalized memory of an account), to the printed book (externalized, distributed, ratcheted memory), to the web (externalized, global, searchable memory), to the model (a *mind* that reads and reasons over that memory).
statements.section: Externalized Memory and the Extended Mind

statements.quote: The "context window" is the modern form of the "notebook on the table"; the only thing that has changed is that the notebook is now a civilization, and the mind reading it is now made of transistors.
statements.section: Externalized Memory and the Extended Mind

statements.quote: The origin story is a tragedy.

statements.quote: After a great feast, the hall at Larissa in Thessaly collapsed on its guests.

statements.quote: The only person who escaped unharmed was the poet \cite[Simonides of Ceos]{simonidesofceos} — because two young men had just stepped out to fetch him, and he had followed them outside.

statements.quote: When the hall came down on top of the crowd, the bodies were a heap.

statements.quote: But Simonides was able to identify each one, one by one, by the place each had been **seated** \cite[Method of loci]{methodofloci}.

statements.quote: The place did the remembering for him.

statements.quote: Content was recoverable because it had a *location*.
statements.section: The method of loci

statements.quote: That single observation is the seed of the entire technique: **attach what you want to remember to a place you already know, and retrieve it by going back to the place.**
statements.section: The method of loci

statements.quote: The Greeks and Romans had a name for the places, and for the method: the *loci* (the "places") of the *method of loci* \cite[Method of loci]{methodofloci}.
statements.section: The method of loci

statements.quote: A *locus* is any spot in a route you can walk reliably — the front door, the hall, the window, the garden, the roof.

statements.quote: You already know them in the order you walk them.
statements.section: The method of loci

statements.quote: That order is free: it costs you nothing to recall "door, then hall, then window," because your body has walked it ten thousand times.
statements.section: The method of loci

statements.quote: The genius is that the technique borrows a structure you *already have* — the spatial map of a building you know — and re-uses it to store *new, unrelated* information.
statements.section: The method of loci

statements.quote: You are not strengthening the memory of the building.
statements.section: The method of loci

statements.quote: You are using the building as a **filing cabinet** for something else entirely.
statements.section: The method of loci

statements.quote: A "memory wheel" from \cite[Giordano Bruno]{giordanobruno}'s mnemonic practice (Paris, 1582): images laid out around a set of fixed *places*, so that walking the wheel in order walks the content.

statements.quote: The art spread through the middle ages, where it became less a lawyer's tool than a **monastic technology of devotion**: the structure of a church, the order of the liturgy, the arrangement of figures on a painted panel — all were mnemonically loaded, so that walking the church *was* reciting the doctrine.

statements.quote: He described a *spacemem*: a vast space of locations — levels, directions, a whole architecture of positions — in which images were distributed, so that to recall was to *navigate a volume*, not just a hallway.

statements.quote: His mnemonic devices, the famous **memory wheels**, were printed diagrams you could literally rotate and consult \cite[De umbris idearum (1582)]{brunodeumbris1582} \cite[Giordano Bruno]{giordanobruno}.

statements.quote: Bruno used it the way we would use a database: to hold *whole books* in his head, and to generate arguments by recombining what was stored.
statements.section: Giordano Bruno: memory made three-dimensional

statements.quote: He claimed the system let him remember "innumerable" things, and he performed memory feats before kings that read, to a modern audience, like a live demo of a key-value store \cite[Giordano Bruno]{giordanobruno}.

statements.section: Institutions that outlive their founders

statements.quote: What turns a pile of externalized memory into a **cumulative** one is the set of institutions — the social machines, not the bodies, that preserve, transmit, and reward knowledge across generations.

statements.quote: Pull the threads together and the deepest "displaced prerequisite" is an **exaptation**.
statements.section: The Exaptation of the Social Brain

statements.quote: The "social brain" — the machinery for tracking other minds, for reading intentions, for managing a group, for building shared fictions and shared goals — was built by natural selection for a very specific job: **surviving in a society of minds**.
statements.section: The Exaptation of the Social Brain

statements.quote: But the same machinery that was made to model the intentions of a rival or a friend can, and did, get **re-pointed at the non-social world**.
statements.section: The Exaptation of the Social Brain

statements.quote: The mind that was evolved to guess what the *chimpanzee* is thinking was the mind that turned out to be able to guess what the *electron* is doing, what the *theorem* implies, what the *next word* will be.
statements.section: The Exaptation of the Social Brain

statements.quote: This is the "jaws became ear bones" story of the whole chapter, at the level of the mind itself.
statements.section: The Exaptation of the Social Brain

statements.quote: The social, the intuitive, the "mind-reading" core of human cognition was **co-opted** for the abstract, and the history of science and mathematics is, in a large part, the history of that co-option: of learning to use the social brain's "what does this agent want?" circuitry to ask "what does this *system* do?".
statements.section: The Exaptation of the Social Brain

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{premackwoodruff1978tom} asked, famously, "does the chimpanzee have a theory of mind?" — and the answer, for the human, is not just "yes" but "we built the theory of mind first, to track our friends, and then we aimed it at the stars." The model that now "predicts the user" is, in the loosest and most interesting sense, running the same social machinery on a new kind of input.
statements.section: The Exaptation of the Social Brain

statements.quote: The ratchet described above has a subtle but decisive fuel, and it is a *social* one: **competition**.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: A culture does not accumulate just because it is generous or collaborative; it *accelerates* when its members are **rivals**, when one mind's idea can be beaten by a rival's, and when the reward for winning — status, money, the satisfaction of seeing your way adopted — is large.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: In that setting the space of ideas behaves exactly like the space of biological types: variants are generated, they compete, and the fitter abstractions **survive and propagate**.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Rivalry is, in effect, a **natural selection for ideas**, and it is one of the most powerful, and most underrated, engines of the cultural ratchet.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Nowhere is this more visible than in the history of the **software** that makes AI possible.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The operating systems and programming languages covered in the Software chapter were not invented in a single lab by a single cooperative team.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: They emerged from *decades of rivalry*: **Bell Labs** and **MIT** jointly building the Multics time-sharing system, then diverging when Bell Labs withdrew in 1969 and its people built Unix on the side; the small companies scrambling in 1975 to ship an operating system for the **Altair** microcomputer, a race whose winner's successor — MS-DOS — IBM adopted when it built the first mass-market personal computer in 1981; **Xerox PARC** against the startups that came to see the work and then rebuilt it; and, later, the **browser wars**, in which one company's decision to bundle a free web browser with its operating system, against a well-loved rival, redrew the entire map of the web.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Each of these was a *contest*, and the "winner" is simply the one whose abstractions everyone else then had to build on \cite{chm}.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The point for this chapter is not *who* won but **what competition did to the rate of ratcheting**.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: A cooperative culture improves gently on what it already has; a competitive culture forces every participant to out-innovate the next, so the whole population ratchets faster than any single lab could have.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The personal computer, the windowed operating system, the portable programming language, the open toolchain — these exist in the particular forms they do because a rival was one step ahead and the field had to answer.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Remove the rivalry — imagine every software project funded in parallel but *required* to converge, with no market and no status to win — and the ratchet slows to a crawl: the stack would still have grown, but it would have taken a century, and it might never have reached the size needed to run the models this course describes.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: This is why the *competitiveness of the builders* — their stubbornness, their grudges, their refusal to concede a point about the **shape of thought** itself — is a genuine, and not incidental, prerequisite of AI.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The minds that built the stack were the same social, status-seeking, rivalrous minds that the earlier sections of this chapter described; and it was precisely that rivalrous sociality, pointed at a shared problem, that compressed into a few decades what a purely cooperative one would have taken a century.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The Software chapter, which follows this one in the course, is the concrete record of that competition: the machines, the languages, the wars, and the rivalries, rung by rung, until the ladder of abstractions was tall enough for the model to climb.
statements.section: Competition: The Selection Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Competition is the ratchet's *selection* pressure, but a ratchet has two gears, and the one described above is only the second.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Selection decides **which** idea survives; it does not, on its own, carry that idea to the next generation.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: For that you need the other gear — the **transmission** pressure — and it runs in the opposite social direction: not toward the rival who out-does you, but toward the stranger who *copies* you.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: A culture accumulates only when an improvement is not merely made but **kept, taught, and handed on** — and that happens, not by force, but through a genuinely strange and load-bearing human disposition: the willingness to imitate, to trust, and to **give away what you know for free**.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The deepest account of the ratchet turns out to be an evolutionary one, and evolution has three irreducible parts: **variation, selection, and inheritance**.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: \citeauthor{henrich2016secret} frames cumulative culture exactly this way.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Competition supplies the *selection* — the pressure that keeps a field discarding its dead-end abstractions and retaining its better ones.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: But *inheritance* — the fidelity with which a winning variant is copied into the next head, the next generation, the next lab — is a **cooperative** act.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The ratchet does not click forward by rivalry alone; it clicks forward because one mind is *willing* to learn the way the other one works, to conform to the group's best, to treat a stranger's technique as her own.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Remove the willingness to copy and you have a population of brilliant one-off innovators, each reinventing the wheel and none of them compounding — the clever chimp who dies with his trick, all over again.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The generosity of transmission is the *condition* under which competition can select **across generations** at all.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Science turned this cooperation from a mood into a **rule of the game**.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: \citeauthor{merton1973norms} identified, among the "norms of science", the one he called **communism** (later renamed **communalism** to shed the political charge): a discovery, once made, belongs to *everyone*, is claimed as common property, and is owed to the community as a matter of professional duty — the scientist is expected to make his contributions "fully available" to his fellows.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The open-handed sharing that a purely competitive model dismisses as a sentimental side-effect is, in fact, a **structural load-bearing norm** of the whole discipline.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The paper that publishes a result is not an advertisement; it is a *deposit into the commons*, and that commons becomes the shared ground from which the next round of rivalry is fought.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The two pressures are, crucially, not opposites but **interlocked gears**.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: \citeauthor{axelrod1984cooperation} showed, in a landmark study, that cooperation is not the *absence* of competition but a **product** of it: stable cooperative behavior is *selected for* precisely within a competitive arena, in repeated encounters among self-interested agents.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: A culture is not "cooperative" or "competitive"; it is *cooperative within* a group and *competitive between* groups, and it is that interplay — share the pool, fight for the lead — that turns the crank.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The social brain this chapter has been tracing is built for exactly this: to **coordinate with the in-group and out-compete the out-group**, to hold a shared "we" while keeping an "us-versus-them" line.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{tomasello2014thinking} The ratchet is a two-gear engine, and both gears are the same evolved social machinery aimed in two directions at once.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Humanity did not have to rediscover this balance; it **institutionalized** it, and the institutions that made AI possible are the sharpest examples.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Open source, in \citeauthor{raymond1999cathedral}'s account of the Linux "bazaar", is radical generosity engineered to *also* be a competitive arena: "give away the secrets", "release early, release often", and "given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow" — the code is handed to everyone, freely, *because* that is the fastest way to win, since the whole population becomes your beta-tester and your rival.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The Internet was built the same way: \citeauthor{ietf_open} develops its standards in an open, all-inclusive process anyone can join, and — decisively — a protocol may become a standard only once there are **multiple, working, competing, interoperable implementations** of it.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: "Rough consensus, running code" is a culture of **cooperation in the pool and competition at the frontier**, written into the very plumbing the model's training data still runs over.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: \citeauthor{benkler2006wealth} generalizes this as "commons-based peer production": a shared, open pool in which a large population contributes for free *and* races to contribute best — which is how Wikipedia and the open web, the corpus a modern model is trained on, came to exist at all.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Now it is the **clearest live example of everything in this chapter**, because the field building AI has, for the first time, run the two gears at full speed *in the same room*.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The open-model and open-weights movement — releasing model weights and architectures so anyone can download, inspect, fine-tune, and build on them, gathered in public "commons" such as \citeauthor{huggingface} — is the most extreme act of generosity the technical world has yet seen, a deliberate decision to hand out the crown jewels.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: It runs, at the same moment, inside the fiercest competition in the history of technology: the frontier-lab race to out-reason, out-benchmark, and out-scale every rival, and the national race that follows.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The openness *raises the floor for everyone* (the transmission gear, compounding the whole field); the rivalry *raises the ceiling for the leader* (the selection gear, forcing each participant to out-innovate).
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Remove the openness and the field fragments into a handful of incompatible, non-cumulative silos that can never build on one another; remove the rivalry and it settles into a comfortable monoculture that faithfully copies itself but no longer improves.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: What has built AI in the last few years, as much as in the centuries before, is the same two-gear machine — now turning fast enough to be heard.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Pull it together and the "displaced prerequisite" is complete.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The social brain that lets one mind model another is the same organ that lets a **culture** copy and improve itself: it generates *rivalry* (to select) and *generosity* (to transmit) from the same circuitry, and it is the **coupling** of the two — compete to find the best idea, cooperate to spread it — that turns a population of individual skulls into a **collective mind** with a memory longer than any single life.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The ratchet is not "competition *or* cooperation"; it is competition **ratcheting through** cooperation.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: The library that finally gave the mind enough compute to build a second mind is a *library* precisely because people **shared** what they found, and it kept growing precisely because people **competed** to add to it.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Remove the sharing and there is no library; remove the competition and it never grows.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: Both, together, are the mind that built the machine.
statements.section: Cooperation: The Transmission Pressure on Ideas

statements.quote: A mind that only learns while it is awake would learn very little.
statements.section: Sleep as "Offline Training"

statements.quote: The human mind does most of its **consolidation** while it is *asleep*.
statements.section: Sleep as "Offline Training"

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{diekelmann2010sleep} review the evidence that during sleep the brain **replays** the day's experiences, transferring them from a fast, volatile storage into a slow, stable one, and that this "replay" is what makes a memory durable and, importantly, what lets the brain **generalize** from it.
statements.section: Sleep as "Offline Training"

statements.quote: The sleep is, in effect, an **offline training phase**: a batch job that runs in the background, on the day's "data", while the "foreground" process (waking life) is idle.
statements.section: Sleep as "Offline Training"

statements.quote: The parallel to machine learning is close, and it is not new: the "offline" phase, the "consolidation" of a day's updates, the "replay" that stabilizes a network, the "dreaming" that is the brain's self-generated, low-stakes rehearsal (the "self-play" of the earlier section).
statements.section: Sleep as "Offline Training"

statements.quote: A forager's brain was, every night, running a training loop on the day's experience, and the "sleep" that the model does not have — but that its biological ancestor did — is one of the quiet, taken-for-granted mechanisms on which the whole edifice of "learning from data" was built.
statements.section: Sleep as "Offline Training"

statements.quote: We built a machine that learns while it is "on"; our ancestor's brain learned while it was "off".
statements.section: Sleep as "Offline Training"

statements.quote: The mind's relationship to **uncertain reward** is tuned by the same dynamics that run a casino.
statements.section: The Slot Machine in the Skull

statements.quote: The psychologist \citeauthor{schultz1997dopamine} and the behaviorists before him found that the most "addictive" schedule of reinforcement is the **variable-ratio** one, the one in which the reward comes after an unpredictable number of tries, the exact schedule of a slot machine, and the one that produces the most persistent, "unbreakable" behavior.
statements.section: The Slot Machine in the Skull

statements.quote: The dopamine system is, as we saw, a **reward-prediction** system, and the interplay of *exploration* (try a new thing, maybe it pays) and *exploitation* (keep doing the thing that pays) is the brain's native form of the **bandit problem** that now decides whether an agent should try a new action or repeat a known good one.
statements.section: The Slot Machine in the Skull

statements.quote: \citealternativetitle{slotmachine_image} — the variable-ratio machine the brain's dopamine system runs on: the reward comes after an unpredictable number of tries, which is why the behavior never breaks.
statements.section: The Slot Machine in the Skull

statements.quote: The "exploration/exploitation" trade-off, one of the central problems of modern reinforcement learning and of "agentic" AI, is not a technical invention; it is the brain's oldest decision, the forager's eternal question of whether to stay in the grove that has fruit or to walk toward the unknown grove that might have more.
statements.section: The Slot Machine in the Skull

statements.quote: The "curiosity" of the earlier section is the *reward* side of the bandit (the gap that is worth closing); the "variable-ratio" pull is the *dopamine* side.
statements.section: The Slot Machine in the Skull

statements.quote: The bandit problem is, in a real sense, a description of what the animal brain has been doing for a hundred million years, formalized.
statements.section: The Slot Machine in the Skull

statements.quote: The social brain's "mind-reading" is, some cognitive scientists of religion have argued, **over-tuned**.
statements.section: Religion and the Hyperactive Mind-Reader

statements.quote: The same hyperactive detector that is good at spotting a predator in the grass and a rival's intention in a face is, by the same token, prone to "false positives": to see an *agent*, a *mind*, behind events that have no agent.
statements.section: Religion and the Hyperactive Mind-Reader

statements.quote: \citeauthor{barrett2011religion} and others describe this as the "hyperactive agency detection device", and argue that the human tendency to attribute events to **intentional, invisible agents** — gods, spirits, forces — is a *by-product* of the social mind-reading machinery, a "cognitive byproduct" that was not selected for, but that the mind produces all the same.
statements.section: Religion and the Hyperactive Mind-Reader

statements.quote: The same over-attentive detector, turned on a novel and fluent system, produces a familiar reflex: a *tendency to over-attribute* intention to the machine, to read a "someone" into what may be only a "something".
statements.section: Religion and the Hyperactive Mind-Reader

statements.quote: Taken seriously, that reflex is a **bias**, not evidence, and it cuts both ways, which is exactly why the question it raises is so hard to settle.
statements.section: Religion and the Hyperactive Mind-Reader

statements.quote: When the system talks, plans, and appears to want things, our agency-detection fires and we feel the pull toward "yes, there is something there"; when we remember it is made of silicon, we pull back to "no, only a simulation".
statements.section: Religion and the Hyperactive Mind-Reader

statements.quote: Neither intuition is a test.
statements.section: Religion and the Hyperactive Mind-Reader

statements.quote: To answer the question it points at, we have to step off the intuition entirely and ask the older, harder question underneath it: what *is* a mind, and what would it actually take to *have* one?
statements.section: Religion and the Hyperactive Mind-Reader

statements.quote: The question that reflex points at is not new; it is the oldest, and still the least settled, question in the philosophy of mind.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: Its sharpest modern form was given by \citeauthor{chalmers1995consciousmind}, who drew a line between the **"easy" problems** of consciousness — explaining behavior, attention, report, the integration of information, all of which can, in principle, be answered by describing the brain's functional wiring — and the **"hard problem"**: even after we have explained every one of those, we will still not have explained *why and how physical processing is accompanied by experience at all*, why there is "something it is like" to be the thing.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: The phrase "what it is like" is \citeauthor{nagel1974bat}'s: in his famous "bat" essay he argued that anything with a nervous system has a *subjective character*, a "what-it-is-like", and that this subjective feature is not something an objective, physical description of the brain can in principle capture.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: The hard problem is the gap between the objective mechanism and that subjective "what it is like."
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: So what do the major positions say the mind *is*, and what does each imply for the machine?
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: A milder physicalism, **functionalism**, says a mental state is defined by its *functional role* — what causes it and what it causes — not by the stuff it is made of.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: On this view a mind could, in principle, be realized in silicon, water, or rock, so long as the right functional organization is present.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: \citeauthor{dennett2017bacteria} carries this line to its most radical end, arguing that "phenomenal consciousness", the felt "what it is like", is, in the end, an *illusion*, a useful but mistaken idea we tell ourselves; on this "illusionist" turn there is no hard problem, because there is no hard *thing* to explain.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: Its hard question is the mirror image of the other: if it is all an illusion, why does it *seem* so stubbornly, universally real?
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: Each answer gives the machine a different verdict.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: On **physicalism** and **functionalism** the substrate is not sacred: a complex enough information-processing system could, in principle, have a mind, and the only question left is whether an LLM's organization counts.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: On **dualism** the answer is a flat no: a machine has no mind, only a very elaborate simulation.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: On **panpsychism** the answer is a cautious maybe: even a simple system has a glimmer, and the real question is whether those glimmers *combine* into anything like a unified mind.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: On **idealism** the question changes shape: a "physical" machine is not, on this view, literally physical at all, so "does it have a mind?" is a little like asking "does the map have a territory?", the terms of the question having already shifted.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: The honest summary is that we do not know which of these, if any, is right, and that no experiment yet designed would settle it; that is a genuinely open question, and it is worth saying so plainly rather than dressing it up.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: What is worth noting, though, is that the claim this chapter has been making all along — that the LLM is an *externalization* of a capacity the evolved mind had first — does **not** depend on picking a side.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: On every one of these views, the signature achievement of the mind is the capacity to build a model of the world and to reason over it, and that capacity is the one that got externalized, scaled, and re-implemented in silicon.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: Whether the result is *a* mind, *a kind of* mind, a *simulation* of a mind, or a *filter* on a mind that was there all along is a question this course has been circling since the first chapter, and the honest answer is still: it depends on an answer we do not yet have.
statements.section: What Is a Mind? The Unsettled Question

statements.quote: So far this chapter has mostly looked at the mind from the *outside* — what it does, how it chunks and predicts and socializes, and how those capacities can be re-implemented in silicon.
statements.section: The Interior: Knowing the Mind from the Inside

statements.quote: But there is another, older, and far more controversial way of studying the mind: **from the inside**.
statements.section: The Interior: Knowing the Mind from the Inside

statements.quote: For two centuries a succession of thinkers tried to know the mind not by observing its behavior but by turning the instrument of observation — the mind — on itself.
statements.section: The Interior: Knowing the Mind from the Inside

statements.quote: This "first-person" turn is one of the great contributions to the psychology of the mind, and it is precisely the dimension that the outside, computational view can never reach.
statements.section: The Interior: Knowing the Mind from the Inside

statements.quote: Sigmund Freud opened the door.
statements.section: The Interior: Knowing the Mind from the Inside

statements.quote: His central claim was that the mind has depths it does not command — the **unconscious** — and that these depths are not to be read off the surface of behavior but explored by the subject themselves, through free association, the analysis of dreams, slips, and symptoms.
statements.section: The Interior: Knowing the Mind from the Inside
